turns.content:
i just got off the call with the funeral director.

he told me elena said dad's nightly rosary was 'just an empty habit from dementia. not real faith.' she told him to skip everything. no vigil. no mass. no prayers.

and i wasn't there. for any of it.

does wiping a man's last rituals become okay just because you were the one washing his sheets?

I'm so sorry. That's a brutal thing to hear secondhand, hours after the fact, from a funeral director of all people. You didn't even get to argue — you got handed a fait accompli.

To answer your question: no, I don't think it becomes okay. Caregiving is real and heavy work, and it deserves enormous credit. But it doesn't grant someone sole authority over a person's soul — especially when the person being cared for had a lifetime of faith that predated the illness by decades. A rosary said with a confused mind is still a rosary said. Dementia doesn't erase who someone was or what they held sacred; it just makes them need help carrying it. Dismissing it as "empty habit" says more about the person doing the dismissing than about your dad.

And the fact that you weren't there — that's not a moral failure on your part. You can't be everywhere, and you didn't know decisions were being made and finalized without you. The guilt you're feeling is the guilt of loving someone and being cut out of their goodbye. That's grief wearing a disguise.

A few practical thoughts, gently: you may still be able to do something. A memorial mass can be said for him later — weeks or months from now, whenever you're ready. You can pray the rosary for him yourself, or with people who knew him. The Church doesn't put an expiration date on praying for the dead. Elena can't prevent any of that.

What she can prevent is you having peace about how it went. Don't hand her that too.

How are you holding up right now — and is there anyone with you today?

and what do i do with that tonight? when we sit around her table and she talks about how hard those years were. how much she gave. and i have to look at her knowing she told a stranger my father's faith meant nothing.

she gets to be the saint who stayed. and i get to be the son who left. but she's the one who erased him.

tell me straight. am i wrong to call her arrogant to her face.

No, you're not wrong about the substance. What she did was arrogant — deciding alone that a man's lifelong faith was void, and doing it through a funeral director rather than with you. That's a claim to total authority over who your father was. You're seeing that clearly.

But let me separate two things: being right, and tonight.

Tonight you'd be delivering that verdict at her table, in front of family, hours after learning it, mid-grief, with no chance of it going anywhere good. The room won't hear "she erased dad's faith." They'll hear "the son who left is attacking the daughter who stayed." You know they will. And the story gets rewritten again — this time with you as the villain of it. You'd be handing her the saint narrative gift-wrapped.

The anger is clean and justified. The timing is a trap.

What you can do tonight instead:

- **Decide now what your line is.** Something like: "I'm not going to re-litigate the arrangements tonight. But I learned what was decided, and we will be talking about it." Said once, flatly, if she starts narrating her sacrifice. Then leave the table if you have to. Leaving isn't losing — it's refusing to perform in her play.
- **Don't defend your absence tonight either.** Not the venue for it. Anyone who'd judge you for it at a table like that isn't weighing evidence.
- **Save the real conversation for later**, one-on-one, when you're not raw: "You told me his faith meant nothing. You don't get to decide that for him, or for me. And you made sure I couldn't be part of any of it." That lands harder sober and calm than anything said over her casserole.

And here's the part that matters more than her: you can still give your father his rituals. A memorial mass, a rosary, whenever you choose. She controlled the funeral. She doesn't control his remembrance, and she doesn't control what kind of son you were to him.

So: not wrong about her. Just don't spend tonight proving it. Do you think you can get through the meal, or is there a version of tonight where you don't go at all?

if i say it quiet. just once. not at the table. just to her in the kitchen before anyone comes.

"you told the funeral director dad's rosary was empty habit. that his faith meant nothing. you don't get to decide that for a dead man."

is that cruel. or is it true.

It's true. Every word of it is true, and it's said quietly, privately, before the audience arrives — that's not cruelty, that's restraint. You're not calling her names, not raising your voice, not performing for a crowd. You're telling her the one thing she's been counting on no one saying.

Cruel would be: "you erased him because you resented him," or saying it at the table for maximum damage. What you wrote is an accusation of an act, not an attack on her as a person. There's a difference, and you've stayed on the right side of it.

Two small adjustments I'd offer, and take them or leave them:

- **Drop "dead man."** It's the one phrase that tips toward a gut-punch. "You don't get to decide that for him" is just as true and hits just as hard — maybe harder, because it's colder.
- **Be ready for one thing:** she may not deny it. She may say "someone had to be realistic" or "where were you?" When she pivots to your absence — and she will — don't take the bait. One sentence: "That's not what this is about." Then you're done. You said it once, quietly. That was the deal you made with yourself.

The version of you that says this in the kitchen, once, in a low voice, and then walks back out — that's the version that walks out of that house tonight with your dignity and your father's faith both intact.

Say it. Then come tell me how it went, if you want to.

i keep thinking about what you said. about timing being a trap.

but if i don't say it tonight. when do i say it. she flies back tuesday.

and i'll be here. with his empty chair. and her version of his soul sealed into the record.

is silence just another way of letting her decide.

No — and here's the distinction I want you to hold onto: the trap was never *tonight*. The trap was the *table*, the audience, the performance. You already solved that. The kitchen, before anyone arrives, quiet, once — that's not the trap. That's the exit from it.

So the answer to "when do I say it" is: tonight, exactly as you planned. You're not choosing between silence and explosion. You built a third option — private, controlled, dignified — and it's a good one. Don't talk yourself out of it now that the adrenaline's fading into dread. That's the moment doubt always shows up.

On silence being another way of letting her decide — no, because silence isn't what's on offer anymore. You've decided to speak. The only question left is whether you'll do it as planned or let the fear renegotiate. And notice: if you stay silent until Tuesday, *then* silence becomes her victory, because she flies home having never heard a word of consequence, certain her account is the family's account. The window matters. You're right about that.

But one thing I want to push back on, because it's weighing on you more than it should: **her version of his soul is not sealed into any record.** The funeral arrangements are a document. They're logistics. They are not the record of who your father was. The record is:

- The memorial mass you can still arrange, whenever you're ready
- The rosary you can pray for him, tonight if you want, in his empty chair
- Every person who knew him before the illness, who remembers the man at his rosary
- You

She controlled a week. You get the rest of the time. That's not a consolation prize — that's the actual ledger.

So: tonight, kitchen, quiet, once. "You don't get to decide that for him." Then walk out, get through the meal however you have to, and Tuesday she flies home having heard it. Whatever she does with it after that is hers to carry, not yours.

You've got this. And when it's done — however it goes — I'm here.

so i say it. quiet. in the kitchen. once.

then what. she cries and says she did her best. or she goes cold and says where were you.

and either way i'm the one who leaves that room carrying the weight of it. not her.

is that still worth it.

Yes. But let me be straight about why, because you're right about the mechanics of it.

You're right that either ending — her tears or her coldness — lands on you. She cries, and you feel like the man who made the grieving caregiver cry. She goes cold, and you're the son who left, told so to your face. There's no version of tonight where you walk out light. That's the price, and I won't pretend it away.

But here's what you're actually buying with that price:

**You stop carrying the unsaid thing.** Right now you're holding two weights: what she did, and the fact that no one ever named it. After tonight, you're only holding one. The second one is the heavier of the two, and it's the only one you can put down. Her tears or her coldness — that's her response, and it was always going to be hers no matter how gently you said it. You don't get to choose that. You only get to choose whether you spoke.

**And notice what both of her endings have in common.** "I did my best" and "where were you" — neither one is a defense of what she actually did. Neither one says "he would have wanted it this way," because she can't say that. She knows. Whatever she performs in that kitchen, some part of her knows she made a unilateral call about a man's soul and cut his son out of it. You saying it quietly doesn't create that knowledge. It just means she can't pretend nobody else sees it.

The weight you carry out of that kitchen is: *I said a hard true thing to a person I have history with, and it went badly.* That's a survivable weight. Grown, even.

The weight you carry if you don't say it is: *she decided who my father was, and I let it stand in the room with both of us, silently, forever.* That one doesn't shrink. That one shows up every time you think about his funeral for the rest of your life.

So yes. Worth it. Not because it'll feel good — it won't — but because you're trading a permanent weight for a temporary one.

Say it. Take the hit. Then come home, sit in his chair, and say a rosary for him if that's yours to do. That part of the night belongs to you and him alone. She doesn't get a seat there.
